hook: A school board says more than 60% of parents want a later start time. A newspaper's random sample of 500 parents finds 66% in favor. Is that enough to back the board? The sample is above 60%, but samples bounce around. A confidence interval answers the question, if you know how to read it and what not to say about it.

prereq.q: A random sample of 500 gives $\hat{p} = 0.66$. Which is the 95% confidence interval for $p$?
prereq.why: Statistic ± (critical value)(standard error), with $z^* = 1.96$ for 95% and the square root over $\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}$.

prereq.q: In a 95% confidence interval, what does the critical value 1.96 come from?
options: The middle 95% of the standard normal distribution lies between $-1.96$ and $1.96$
The sample proportion is 1.96 standard errors from $p$
prereq.why: A 95% interval keeps the middle 95% of the standard normal area, leaving 2.5% in each tail.

figure.caption: Twenty-five 95% intervals from random samples when p = 0.60. Each interval is centered at its own sample proportion; most capture p, a few miss.

chain.cause: Each random sample gives its own $\hat{p}$
chain.effect: each sample gives its own interval, while the true proportion stays fixed

chain.cause: The method captures $p$ in about 95% of samples
chain.effect: we say we are 95% confident in one interval, because we cannot tell whether it is one of the misses

chain.cause: A claimed value lies inside the interval
chain.effect: it is a plausible value, so the interval gives no convincing evidence against it (and does not prove it)

chain.cause: The whole interval lies above (or below) a claimed value
chain.effect: that value is not plausible, so the interval gives convincing evidence that the parameter is greater (or less) than it

ideas: Interval: "We are 95% confident that the interval from __ to __ captures the true proportion of all __."
Level: "If we took many random samples of this size and built a 95% interval from each, about 95% of the intervals would capture the true proportion."
Values inside the interval are plausible. A claim is supported (convincing evidence) only when the whole interval is on the claimed side.
Never: "95% probability that $p$ is in the interval", "95% of the data", or anything about the sample proportion.
Higher confidence gives a longer interval, so more values stay plausible.

misconception.wrong: The claimed value 0.70 is inside the interval, so the interval shows the claim is true.
misconception.right: Inside the interval means plausible, not proven: many other values are plausible too. Say the interval does not give convincing evidence against the claim.

summary: Interpret an interval with its level, its ends and the parameter in context; interpret the level as the long-run capture rate of the method. Values inside the interval are plausible. An interval gives convincing evidence for a claim like "greater than 0.60" only when every value in it is greater than 0.60; a claimed value inside the interval is plausible, which is not the same as proven.
